source_metadata.title: Blood pressure and glycaemic effects of dapagliflozin versus placebo in patients with type 2 diabetes on combination antihypertensive therapy: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 study

atoms.canonical_statement: The study aimed to compare the blood-pressure and glycaemic effects of dapagliflozin with placebo in patients with inadequately controlled type 2 diabetes and hypertension already receiving combination antihypertensive therapy.
The trial was a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 study.
Participants were enrolled at 311 centres in 16 countries across five continents.
Randomization assigned patients 1:1 to dapagliflozin 10 mg once daily or placebo using an interactive voice-response system.
Randomization was stratified by the class of the additional antihypertensive drug and by baseline insulin use, using a block size of two.
Eligible participants were 18 to 89 years old.

atoms.canonical_statement: The protocol initially included lower dapagliflozin dose arms, but enrolment to the 5 mg dose was stopped by amendment and 133 randomized 5 mg patients were excluded from the main 10 mg versus placebo efficacy analysis.
Blood-pressure measurements were standardized after a resting period, and 24-hour ambulatory blood-pressure monitoring was used for ambulatory endpoints.
The two co-primary endpoints were tested within a hierarchical closed-testing procedure to control type I error.
Primary efficacy analyses used repeated-measures models, while 24-hour ambulatory systolic blood pressure was analysed with ANCOVA.
The sample-size plan targeted 408 patients, approximately 204 per group, allowing for about 5% missing data.
The sample-size assumptions provided at least 80% power to detect a 4 mm Hg between-group systolic blood-pressure difference assuming SD 14 mm Hg.
The sample-size assumptions provided at least 94% power to detect a 0.4 percentage-point HbA1c difference assuming SD 1.1 percentage points.

Blood-pressure measurements obtained after antihypertensive rescue were excluded from efficacy analyses, whereas HbA1c, uric acid, fasting glucose, and bodyweight measurements after rescue remained included.
The safety analysis set included all randomized patients who received at least one dose of study treatment.
Change from baseline to week 12 in seated systolic blood pressure was a co-primary endpoint.

Achieving seated blood pressure below 130/80 mm Hg was an exploratory blood-pressure-control endpoint.
Safety assessment included adverse events, serious adverse events, adverse events of special interest, orthostatic hypotension, and laboratory measures.

At week 12, seated systolic blood pressure decreased by 11.90 mm Hg with dapagliflozin and 7.62 mm Hg with placebo; the adjusted placebo-corrected difference was −4.28 mm Hg (95% CI −6.54 to −2.02; p=0.0002).

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors concluded that dapagliflozin 10 mg significantly improved blood pressure and HbA1c and was tolerated similarly to placebo.
The authors interpreted the blood-pressure-lowering effect as particularly favourable among patients whose additional antihypertensive drug was a β blocker or calcium-channel blocker.
The authors proposed that dapagliflozin could add a diuretic-like effect to antihypertensive regimens in patients with type 2 diabetes needing better blood-pressure control.
The authors identified the strict entry criteria and large number of study sites as limitations affecting interpretation.
The antihypertensive-class subgroup analyses were post hoc and based on relatively small subgroup samples.
The authors noted that the smaller systolic blood-pressure effect in the thiazide subgroup could reflect chance or a greater placebo response rather than true treatment-effect heterogeneity.
Few participants had moderate renal impairment, limiting inference for patients with lower kidney function.
The 12-week study was not designed to assess major cardiovascular outcomes.
The study was funded by Bristol-Myers Squibb and AstraZeneca.
The funders participated in study design, data collection, data analysis, data interpretation, and the decision to submit the report for publication.
Several authors were employees and/or shareholders of AstraZeneca or Bristol-Myers Squibb, and the corresponding author reported research funding and consulting relationships with industry.
